newsitem.title: USA: Mitchell seen as top candidate to head State Dept.
newsitem.headline: Mitchell seen as top candidate to head State Dept.

text.p: Former Sen. George Mitchell was moving ahead in the contest to succeed Warren Christopher as secretary of state, officials said on Thursday.

While they do not rule out U.N. Ambassador Madeleine Albright, who many assumed not long ago was the leading candidate, or some other appointee, the officials said Mitchell's name is now the one most often mentioned.
"It looks like Mitchell," one official told Reuters, although he said the decision did not yet seem locked up.
President Bill Clinton, hailing Christopher at the White House, sidestepped a reporter's query on who the successor would be.

Ultimately in the often byzantine world of selecting a a Cabinet, the answer will only be known for sure when Clinton makes the announcement. Officials say that is expected next week, before Clinton leaves on a trip to Asia.
Choices often depend on who gets other jobs. Pressure may not be so great to name a woman at state, for instance, if Clinton keeps Janet Reno as attorney general.
But the infighting is proceeding apace, with National Security Adviser Anthony Lake's struggle to remain in his current job said to play a major role in the calculations.

Mitchell, the former majority leader when Democrats controlled the Senate, has worked closely with Lake in forging an unusually direct U.S. role in Northern Ireland. Mitchell was invited in June by Britain and Ireland to chair Northern Ireland peace talks, but they have so far made no progress.

Officials said Mitchell -- who is akin to Christopher in his patience and determination -- gained in the secretary of state sweepstakes by helping Clinton prepare for presidential campaign debates. Mitchell played Republican rival Bob Dole.
Knowing Congress, he could be valuable in what is expected to be an uphill Clinton push to reverse spending cuts that have hurt Washington's ability to conduct diplomacy.
In Belfast on Wednesday, Mitchell played down reports he might be named secretary of state but said: "If I am offered that or anything else I will consider it at the time."

Albright arguably has more hands-on foreign policy experience and broader knowledge of the subject matter. She has loyally pressed Clinton's policies at the United Nations and proved an articulate and passionate spokeswoman for U.S. interests.
But foreign policy elites do not consider her a "heavyweight" in the field.

Critics say she does not have Mitchell's "stature" and could have problems getting approved by the Senate. Whereas Mitchell's political career is seen as a boon, Albright's time advising Democratic candidates like Clinton and others is not viewed as positively, they said.

As for Lake, officials said it was made clear he could be appointed ambassador to a major country. But Lake in recent weeks has put up an increasingly feisty and vocal fight to keep the post that he has held for four years, they said.

The National Security Adviser, who has close and frequent daily contact with the president, coordinates national security policy among relevant agencies, including the State and Defence departments and the Central Intelligence Agency.

Lake was understood to want to be secretary of state. But apparently concluding that would not happen, he has dug in at the National Security Council and was pushing for Mitchell to be Christopher's successor, the officials said.

Until recently, officials said, many assumed Albright would be named the first female secretary of state in U.S. history, Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott would replace Lake and former Bosnia negotiator Richard Holbrooke would take Albright's job at the United Nations.

But with Lake refusing to leave his post, that blocks the way for the appointment of Talbott -- an old Clinton friend from their days at Oxford University and the administration's top Russia policymaker -- as national security adviser.

Talbott could conceivably stay on as the State Department's number two under a new secretary. But the only national security promotion open to him appears to be national security adviser, as it does not require Senate confirmation.
Chairman Jesse Helms of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, a Republican, promised anew on Thursday that Talbott would face a fight if he was named to a Senate-approved job.
Helms, from North Carolina, has faulted Talbott for being too supportive of Russian President Boris Yeltsin and for writings critical of Israel when Talbott was a journalist.
Talbott is said to back Albright for secretary of state. But some officials said Lake is a far better bureaucratic infighter than Talbott, who one insider called "too nice."

Christopher discussed possible successors with Clinton earlier in the week. In an interview on Thursday, Christopher said that whoever is chosen must provide forceful, steady and determined leadership on U.S. foreign policy.
